essential: Date and setting: 2 p.m., May 7, 1915. The Lusitania has been torpedoed twice and is sinking, and women and children are lined up for the boats.
An unnamed young girl, no more than eighteen, stands alone and unafraid, with grave, steadfast eyes.
The man is a first-class passenger she has noticed. He is mysterious and avoids people. He glances suspiciously over his shoulder and is now agitated with fear, yet he does not seem afraid of death.
He asks whether she is American, then whether she is patriotic. She flushes indignantly ('I guess…'), which gives her American idiom.
He explains that he is carrying vitally important papers that may matter to the Allies, and that they have more chance with a woman.
He warns there may be danger if he has been followed, though he doesn't think he has. She accepts ('real proud to be chosen').
Instructions: watch for a 'Shipmate' advertisement in the Times. If nothing appears within three days, deliver the packet into the American Ambassador's own hands.
He says goodbye loudly as cover. The packet passes palm to palm, and she goes to the boat as the ship lists.
Do not name the girl or the man.
optional: Detail of women clinging to husbands and children (p1 middle).
'He spoke to no one… rebuff the overture' can be condensed into one clause.
'Quite clear' exchange (p20) and his 'Is that clear?'
The final list-to-starboard sentence can be compressed, but she must still go to the boat.

essential: Tuppence's initial suspicion of the stranger's motive is dispelled. She dislikes him instinctively: a big, clean-shaven man with a heavy jowl and small, shifty eyes.
He overheard them in Lyons' and followed her. His card reads Mr. Edward Whittington, Esthonia Glassware Co. He sets an appointment for 11 tomorrow.
Her terrier-like shake of the shoulders, and her resolve.
She telegraphs Tommy at his club, using his retained pencil: 'Don't put in advertisement. Will explain to-morrow.' She weighs ninepence against five shillings.
Office: a dirty outer office with a middle-aged clerk, then a private room. Whittington is sleek and shifty.

The offer: £100 plus expenses for three months at Madame Colombier's pensionnat in Paris, as his ward, with no contact with friends and absolute secrecy. He suggests she pass as an American, given her picked-up accent, from an American hospital pal.
She says the terms are too liberal, and he gives his justification. She insists her partner Beresford comes too: 'both or neither'.
Asked her name, she blurts 'Jane Finn' to protect her father. He reacts with purple rage and dismay, believes she has been playing him, and asks 'Rita?'
Her truthful bluffs: 'Rita knows nothing about me', 'Very little indeed', 'It might be my own name', 'by chance'. Each one increases his unease.
She plays the adventuress ('live by my wits'). Keep 'Blackmail, eh?' answered by 'payment of services in advance', and his grudging admiration.
The clerk brings a 'telephone message'. Whittington dismisses 'Brown', defers the meeting to the same time tomorrow and pays £50. His renewed geniality gives her a faint misgiving.
She takes a taxi to meet Tommy at five to twelve and makes the five-pound-note line.
optional: Dream of Esthonia Glassware as hospital plates (p28).
Walking up the street to avoid looking eager, and taking the stairs (p29–30).

'Gay deceiver' aside (p46).

essential: Taxi fare scramble: Tommy's limited coins and the driver's protest. Tuppence claims nothing smaller than a fiver, and the truth isn't believed.
She proposes extravagant lunch spots and an absurd menu. Tommy is incredulous, and she waves five-pound notes. They lunch at the Piccadilly grill room.

She tells the story and says she invented 'Jane Finn'. Tommy corrects her: he told her the name. One of the two men he overheard was big, fat, clean-shaven and dark, so Tuppence identifies Whittington. Tommy did not notice the other man.
Tommy turns serious: she can't bluff forever, and it may be actionable blackmail. She rebuts with her definition of blackmail.

Tuppence's plan: she goes alone tomorrow to stall Whittington, while Tommy, whom Whittington barely saw, waits outside and follows him on her signal. Tommy objects to 'one young man is much like another' ('the second time').
Tommy limits her spending plans. They have dinner and a show, and two fivers are spent.
Next morning the office is shut. A clerk says the company closed yesterday afternoon and is being wound up, the office is to let, and no address is known.
Tuppence argues their flight proves the Jane Finn business matters: 'sleuths in earnest'. Tommy notes there's no one left to sleuth.
She borrows the pencil and writes the new ad, signed Y. A.
